what: O'Reilly Automotive sells car parts. It runs more than 6,000 stores serving both professional repair shops and people fixing their own cars, and keeps a deep inventory close to customers so a mechanic can get a part within the hour.
customers: Independent repair shops and service chains, plus consumers doing their own repairs.
money: parts sold to repair shops, delivered quickly from local stores and hubs
parts and accessories sold directly to consumers
moat: A distribution network of hubs and stores that can deliver an unusual part the same day, which online sellers cannot match for urgent repairs.
risks: Electric vehicles need fewer replacement parts over time
Debt of about $10 billion was taken on to fund buybacks
Mild weather reduces failures and therefore demand
Growth depends on opening new stores in a maturing market
opportunities: The average US vehicle is older than ever, which raises repair demand
Return on invested capital near 35% is exceptional for a retailer
It has shrunk its share count heavily through continuous buybacks
watch: Comparable store sales split between professional and do-it-yourself customers.
